title: BYTE-GOLD: mine, label, plant
bridge: BYTE-GOLD is like a Playwright test suite for Byte: a fixed set of PRs with known answers, run before a change ships. Except the answers are human judgements, written by hand. And Byte must never see them, so the set lives in a repo Byte cannot read.
intro: Byte reviews every fcp PR, but today nobody can say how many real bugs it catches. This lesson builds BYTE-GOLD, a fixed set of 240 PRs with known answers, from fcp's own history. A script mines the bugs, the guilds confirm them and write the answers, and they plant 60 more.

steps.text: gives the keys of Bug tickets resolved in the last 540 days
each fix commit on main is blamed line by line
writes about 300 real-bug candidates and about 150 clean PRs
Sean splits the list by area; a labeler takes a batch

checks the severities are consistent, then merges

sections.h: A fix commit on fcp main
p: Open your fcp clone and run `git log --oneline main | head`. Every line looks like `[FE] RH-6589: ... (#2445)`: fcp squash-merges, so one PR becomes one commit, and the subject ends with the PR number. When a Jira Bug is fixed, its fix lands as one of these commits, with the RH key in the subject.

The fix changed some lines. Whoever wrote those lines before the fix most likely introduced the bug. `git blame` names, for every line of a file, the commit that last wrote it. That commit's subject ends with `(#NNNN)`, so blame gives us the introducing PR, the PR Byte should have caught.

This is the SZZ method, named after the three researchers who published it. It is not perfect: a fix can touch lines the bug never lived in. That is why people confirm every candidate before it becomes a case. A candidate is a PR the script thinks introduced a bug; a case is a candidate a person confirmed and labelled.

The cases and their answers live in a new private repo, `RhinoHealth/byte-gold` (name to confirm with DevOps). Access is Sean, Nave and the labelers. The Byte App is never installed on it: installed repos get repinned and reviewed, and Byte must never see the answers.

callout.text: Byte never reads byte-gold. Not through the App, not through a mounted folder, not through a prompt. The moment it does, every score is worthless.

sections.h: The miner, part 1: patterns and git
p: The script is `scripts/gold-mine.ts` in RhinoHealth/byte, next to `scripts/sniff-fixtures.ts`. It runs on an operator's laptop, never in CI. It needs a full fcp clone, `gh` and a read-only Jira token in the environment. The sketch is 30 lines, so it comes in two blocks; nothing is removed between them.

Three regular expressions do the matching. A hunk is one block of changed lines in a diff. Its header looks like `@@ -212,7 +212,8 @@`. The `-212,7` part is the old-side start line and how many old lines the block covers.
sections.because: We match fcp's commit subjects and skip files that cannot carry a shipped bug, so the blame counts only real code.

notes.text: A comment that says where this runs: on a laptop, never in CI. It needs things CI must not have, like a Jira token.
The command to run it: tsx runs TypeScript directly, `--fcp` is the clone, `--since 540d` the window, `--out` the byte-gold candidates folder.
execFileSync runs a program with an argument list and waits. No shell string, so a strange file name cannot become a command (lesson p1-2).
Matches `(#2445)` at the very end of a subject and captures the number. The `$` anchors it to the end, so a number in the middle does not count.
Paths to skip: test folders, lockfiles and generated gRPC stubs (`*_pb2.py`). A fix there is not a shipped bug in product code.
Pulls the old-side start line and the optional line count out of a hunk header. When the count is missing, the hunk covers one line.
A small helper: `git -C <clone> <args>` runs git inside the fcp clone and returns its output as a string.
maxBuffer is raised to 256 MiB because a diff or blame of a big file can exceed Node's default and throw.
The one-line idea of SZZ. Blame the old-side lines at the fix's parent commit; the blamed commits point at the introducing PR.

p: The second block is the function itself, lines 13 to 30 of the sketch. It takes the clone path and one fix commit SHA. It returns a Map from PR number to the number of blamed lines. Porcelain is git's name for an output format meant for programs, stable across versions, which is why we ask blame for it.

`${fixSha}^` is the fix commit's parent: the code as it was right before the fix. We diff from the parent to the fix with `-U0`, which means zero context lines, so every hunk holds only changed lines. Then we blame the parent for exactly those line ranges.
sections.because: We blame the parent because blaming the fix's own lines would name the fix PR, not the bug's author.

notes.text: Exported so a test, or the lab, can call it with a scratch repo and one SHA. The Map keys are PR numbers.
The count per PR. A PR blamed for ten of the fixed lines is a stronger candidate than one blamed for one.
The diff from the parent to the fix, zero context, split into lines. We walk it once and keep track of the current file.
A `--- a/<path>` line starts a new file in the diff. `slice(6)` drops the `--- a/` prefix and keeps the path.
The old-side line count from the hunk header, defaulting to 1 when the header has no comma part.
Skip when the line is not a hunk header, when the path is in SKIP, or when the hunk removed nothing. A pure addition has no old lines to blame.
Blame only the range `-L<from>,<to>` at the parent. `-w` ignores whitespace, `-M` and `-C` follow moved and copied lines, so a reformat does not take the blame.
In porcelain output each blamed line starts with a 40-character SHA followed by two numbers. The regex collects those SHAs; `?? []` handles no match.
`git log -1 --format=%s <sha>` prints that commit's subject; PR_IN_SUBJECT pulls the PR number out of it.
A commit without `(#N)` gives NaN, and `NaN > 0` is false, so it is ignored. Otherwise add one blamed line to that PR.
The Map goes back to the caller, which scores it and writes one JSON line per candidate.
The shape of a row in candidates/real.jsonl: ids and numbers only, plus the Jira key. Never the ticket text.

sections.ifInstead: If instead you see `fatal: file ... has only N lines`, the range came from the new side. Check that HUNK reads the `-a,b` part of the header, not the `+c,d` part.

sections.h: From blame to candidates and a clean pool
p: The script first needs the fix commits. The JQL `project = RH AND issuetype = Bug AND statusCategory = Done AND resolved >= -540d` gives the keys. We match those keys in squash subjects. Add every `Revert "..."` commit, and subjects containing fix or hotfix, since not every fix names a ticket.

Each candidate gets a score from three things. How many of its lines the fix blamed, the days from its merge to the fix, and the PR size. PRs over 2,000 changed lines are dropped; nobody can label those. We aim for about 300 candidates so that about 120 survive confirmation.

A clean PR is one that never caused a bug, and the script builds a pool of those too. The rule: merged 90 to 365 days ago, under 600 changed lines, never blamed by any fix, never reverted. About 150 of them. Clean PRs are how we measure false alarms, findings on code that had nothing wrong.
The output is `candidates/real.jsonl`, `candidates/clean.jsonl` and a `case.json` template in byte-gold's README. Rows hold ids, numbers and the Jira key only.

callout.text: Keep the Jira key, never the ticket text. Bug tickets can name customers, and a judge model reads byte-gold files later (lesson g2-2).

p: Now people take over. Sean splits `candidates/real.jsonl` by area: `frontend/` and `ohif/` go to the FE guild, `cloud/`, `client/`, `sdk/` and `common/` to the BE guild. He posts a sign-up list in each guild channel, and the budget is about 10 minutes per candidate.

For each candidate the labeler opens three things: the fix PR, the Jira Bug and the introducing PR. Keep the candidate only if the cause is visible in the introducing PR's diff. Otherwise mark it rejected with one word: refactor, config or unclear.

A kept candidate becomes `cases/<id>/case.json`, filled from the README template. Its `golden` list holds the golden comment: where the bug is, how bad it is, and what a reviewer should have said. The numbers in the sketch are made up.
sections.because: One fixed file shape lets the packer and the scorer in lesson g2-2 read every case the same way, whoever wrote it.

code.text:
{
  "id": "real-0042",
  "kind": "real",
  "repository": "RhinoHealth/fcp",
  "prNumber": 1874,
  "team": "be",
  "bugKey": "RH-8123",
  "fixPr": 1932,
  "blankBody": false,
  "split": null,
  "golden": [
    {
      "path": "cloud/rhinoCloud/rhinoCore/permissions.py",
      "startLine": 212,
      "endLine": 218,
      "severity": "high",
      "defect": "The new object check compares the user's active workgroup instead of the dataset's own workgroup, so a member of another workgroup can read the dataset.",
      "labeler": "<labeler's GitHub login>"
    }
  ]
}

notes.text: The case id is the folder name: `real-` plus a number. It is also the key the gate hashes to assign splits later.
`real` means a bug from history. The other kinds are `clean` and `planted` (next section).
The introducing PR, the one Byte will review in the replay. Not the fix PR.
The Jira key and nothing else from the ticket. The ticket text can name customers.
The fix PR, kept so a reviewer of the batch can check the story in one click.
Set to true when the PR's title or body were edited later and now mention the bug. The packer then leaves the body out.
Left null by the labeler. Lesson g2-2 assigns `dev` or `holdout` once, by a stable hash of the id.
The file and the line range where the bug lives, on the introducing PR's head. The scorer accepts a finding within 10 lines of this range.
Byte's severity scale: high means you would block the merge, medium is real but not blocking, low is minor.
The defect in one or two sentences about the code only: no customer names, no ticket text, no data from the Bug. A judge model reads this.
Who labelled it, by GitHub login, so Sean can ask about a severity that looks off.

p: Clean cases come from `candidates/clean.jsonl`. The labeler skims the diff and the code's later history and keeps the PR if nobody ever found a defect in it. Its `case.json` has `kind: clean` and an empty `golden` list. The bar for Byte on these is at most 0.2 high or medium findings per clean PR.

A planted bug is a small patch a person writes on top of a different clean PR, adding exactly one bug. History gives too few of some bug classes, so we plant them. The README lists the classes. Missing permission or workgroup check, unhandled status, swallowed error, off-by-one, N+1 query. Also a migration that locks a big table, a removed export still in use, and unsafe HTML.

The patch is saved as `cases/<id>/planted.patch` and must pass `git apply --check` on the PR head. Make it look like the code around it: no hinting comments, no TODOs, no odd names. Fake data only: never real dataset names, patient-like values or customer names.
sections.because: A planted case points at a patch file, so the packer can apply it on the PR head before Byte looks.

code.text:
{
  "id": "planted-0017",
  "kind": "planted",
  "repository": "RhinoHealth/fcp",
  "prNumber": 2190,
  "team": "fe",
  "plantedPatch": "planted.patch",
  "plantedClass": "missing-workgroup-scope",
  "blankBody": false,
  "split": null,
  "golden": [
    {
      "path": "<the frontend file planted.patch edits>",
      "startLine": 41,
      "endLine": 44,
      "severity": "high",
      "defect": "The query key no longer includes the workgroup, so after a workgroup switch the page shows the previous workgroup's cached datasets.",
      "labeler": "<labeler's GitHub login>"
    }
  ]
}

notes.text: `planted`: the bug is not in the PR as merged; it is added by the patch below.
A clean PR, different from the ones kept as clean cases, so one PR is never both.
The patch file next to this case.json. The packer applies it on the head before building the tree.
The bug class from the README list, as a short slug, so the scorecard can show recall per class.
Same meaning as for real cases; usually false, because the original PR never mentioned this bug.
The file the patch edits. The placeholder is here because the sketch is a template; you write the real path.
The lines the patch changed on the head, so a finding can be matched to them.
Again, the defect in code terms only. Here: a cache key dropped the workgroup, so a stale list shows after a switch.

sections.h: Batches, review, and what never goes in
p: Labelers open one byte-gold PR per batch. Sean reviews each batch for consistent severities. The same kind of defect must get the same level from an FE and a BE labeler. The budget is about 10 minutes per clean PR and 20 per planted bug.

The targets are 120 confirmed real bugs, 60 clean PRs and 60 planted bugs, 240 cases in all. Stop at 120 real; leftover candidates wait for next quarter. The plan gives 4 days to labelling, which is probably tight for 240 cases, so watch the pace in week 3.

Three things never enter byte-gold: customer names, ticket text, and patient-like values. Byte's App is never installed, and no replay ever mounts the repo (lesson g2-2). Today Byte has no review-quality eval at all, only the sniff fixtures, so this set is the first number anyone can defend.

callout.text: When two labelers disagree on severity, ask: would you block the merge? Yes is high. Real but you would merge is medium. Everything else is low.

mkdir -p cases/real-0001 and write cases/real-0001/case.json by hand in the G2-02 shape. Use id real-0001, kind real, repository lab/gold-lab, prNumber 12, bugKey RH-1, fixPr 15, blankBody false, split null. One golden entry: src/greet.ts lines 2 to 2, severity medium, a one-sentence defect, your login as labeler. Then: jq '.kind, .prNumber, (.golden | length)' cases/real-0001/case.json

lab.faded: Same task, one more commit pair. Add tests/greet.test.ts in a commit whose subject ends with (#13). Then change one line of it in a commit "[BE] RH-2: fix test expectation (#16)" and run scripts/run.ts again. The step left out: say which line of gold-mine.ts makes the output Map(0) {}, and why.
lab.alone: Plant a bug. Check out the (#15) commit and edit src/greet.ts so the bug is back (drop the .trim() call). Save `git diff` as cases/planted-0001/planted.patch, restore the file and return to main. Write cases/planted-0001/case.json with kind planted, plantedPatch planted.patch and a golden comment on the changed line. `git apply --check cases/planted-0001/planted.patch` must print nothing and exit 0.
lab.done: scripts/run.ts prints Map(1) { 12 => 1 }, jq reads your case.json, and git apply --check accepts planted.patch with no output.

quiz.q: Which commit does gold-mine.ts blame to find the introducing PR?

options.text: The fix commit's parent, on the old-side lines the fix changed
options.why: Those lines are the code as it was before the fix, so blame names who wrote the bug.

options.text: The fix commit itself, on the lines it added
options.why: Added lines were written by the fix, so blame would point at the fix PR every time.

options.text: The newest commit on main, so moved code is followed
options.why: Later edits would take the blame; -M and -C already follow moves at the parent.

quiz.q: A labeler opens a candidate and cannot see the cause in the introducing PR's diff. What next?

options.text: Write the golden comment on the fix PR instead
options.why: Byte reviews the introducing PR in the replay; a comment on the fix PR can never be matched.

options.text: Mark it rejected with one word, such as unclear, and move on
options.why: The ticket allows about 10 minutes per candidate; a vague answer key is worse than a smaller one.

options.text: Keep it with severity low so the number of cases stays at 120
options.why: A wrong case makes recall wrong; stop at 120 confirmed, leftovers wait for next quarter.

quiz.q: What goes into case.json for a real bug?

options.text: The Jira ticket's description, so the judge has full context
options.why: Bug tickets can name customers; byte-gold holds the key only.

options.text: The customer-facing error text copied from the Bug
options.why: That is ticket text too, and a judge model reads this file.

options.text: The Jira key, the PR numbers, and a defect sentence about the code only
options.why: Ids, numbers and a code-only defect sentence are all the packer, scorer and judge need.

words.plain: A method that blames the lines a fix changed to find the change that introduced the bug.
git blame names, for each line of a file, the commit that last wrote it.
One block of changed lines in a diff, with a header like @@ -212,7 +212,8 @@.
Git's stable, program-friendly output format, asked for with --porcelain.
A PR the miner thinks introduced a bug, or a PR it thinks is clean, before a person checks it.
The answer for one case: the file and lines of the bug, its severity, and the defect in code terms.
One bug a person adds to a clean PR with a small patch, so a bug class has enough cases.

tickets.why: This lesson showed how blame at the fix's parent turns a fixed Bug ticket into the PR that introduced it.
walk: Ask DevOps for the private repo RhinoHealth/byte-gold (name to confirm), with access for Sean, Nave and the labelers. Never install the Byte App on it.
Add scripts/gold-mine.ts to RhinoHealth/byte next to scripts/sniff-fixtures.ts, with the two blocks above. It runs on a laptop with a full fcp clone, gh and a read-only Jira token, never in CI.

Collect fix commits on fcp main. The JQL is `project = RH AND issuetype = Bug AND statusCategory = Done AND resolved >= -540d`. Match the keys in squash subjects; add every `Revert "..."` commit and subjects with fix or hotfix.
For each fix call introducingPrs: it blames the old-side lines at `<fix>^` with `git blame -w -M -C --porcelain`. Tests, lockfiles and *_pb2.py are skipped.
Score candidates by blamed lines, days from merge to fix and PR size. Drop PRs over 2,000 changed lines; aim for about 300 candidates.
Build the clean pool: merged 90 to 365 days ago, under 600 changed lines, never blamed, never reverted (about 150).
Write candidates/real.jsonl, candidates/clean.jsonl and the case.json template in byte-gold's README, with the Jira key only, never ticket text.

tickets.why: This lesson explained the case.json shape and the severity scale the golden comments use.
walk: Sean splits candidates/real.jsonl by area: frontend/ and ohif/ to the FE guild; cloud/, client/, sdk/ and common/ to the BE guild. He posts a sign-up list in each guild channel.
Per candidate, open the fix PR, the Jira Bug and the introducing PR. Keep it only if the cause is visible in the introducing PR's diff; else reject with one word (refactor, config, unclear).
Fill cases/<id>/case.json from the README template; severity high blocks the merge, medium is real but not blocking, low is minor.
Describe the code defect only: no customer names, ticket text or data from the Bug.
If the introducing PR's title or body were edited later and mention the bug, set blankBody to true.
Open one byte-gold PR per batch; Sean reviews for consistent severities; stop at 120 confirmed.

tickets.why: This lesson showed what a clean case and a planted case look like, and why clean PRs measure false alarms.
walk: For each row in candidates/clean.jsonl, skim the diff and the code's later history. Keep it if nobody found a defect, with kind clean and an empty golden list.
For a planted case, take a different clean PR. Write a small patch on its head adding one bug from the README's class list.
Save it as cases/<id>/planted.patch; it must pass `git apply --check` on the PR head. Write case.json with kind planted and the golden comment.
Make the planted code look like its surroundings: no hinting comments, no TODOs, no odd names; fake data only.
Budget about 10 minutes per clean PR and 20 per planted bug; one byte-gold PR per batch for Sean to review.

remember: BYTE-GOLD's answers come from fcp's own history and from people, and Byte never sees them.
